what_it_proves: Dollar General is a massive local-access network.
boundary: Store count proves reach, not customer loyalty or store-level cash quality.

what_it_proves: Revenue recovered while the company worked through operating cleanup.
boundary: Sales growth does not separate traffic, ticket, price, mix, or new-store contribution by itself.

what_it_proves: The business handles a large amount of essential and small-basket spending.
boundary: Large sales do not prove lower-income consumer health or durable margin.

what_it_proves: Existing stores improved, not only new stores.
boundary: Same-store sales do not prove whether traffic or ticket drove the improvement.
EPS growth can reflect cost actions, buybacks, tax, or other factors and is not store-level cash proof.

what_it_proves: Profitability was visible at the shareholder level.
boundary: EPS is not operating cash flow and does not prove inventory or shrink control by itself.

what_it_proves: The business is heavily tied to recurring necessities.
boundary: Consumables can drive traffic while pressuring margin, so mix is not automatically positive.

what_it_proves: Customers need nearby small-basket replenishment when cash, time, or transportation are constrained.
boundary: A plausible customer mechanism is not cohort-level proof without basket and income evidence.

what_it_proves: Proximity and repeat trips are the core operating loop.
boundary: The mechanism fails if store standards, shrink, labor, inventory, or mix erode economics.

what_it_proves: Store visits improved in the current quarter.
boundary: Traffic growth does not prove ticket quality, basket margin, or durable customer health.

what_it_proves: Unit economics improved rather than only traffic.
boundary: Gross-margin improvement does not prove shrink, labor, or inventory issues are permanently solved.

what_it_proves: The margin level was visible after improvement.
boundary: Gross margin is before many operating costs and is not full cash conversion proof.
